constitutive_assumptions: Hooke's law governs the mechanical response and axial tension of the twisted multi-strand cable with an elastic coefficient k.
All mechanical work input by the motor torque is converted entirely into elastic potential energy of the cable without energy losses.
Equal-volume cylinder deformation assumption (V0 = Vtwisted) was evaluated and identified as inaccurate for multi-strand cables due to inter-strand gap closure during initial twisting.
The multi-substrate continuum assembly behaves as an equivalent cantilever beam with a modified structural stiffness coefficient (adjusted from 3 to 2) to account for discrete matrix interactions.
Circumferential drive cables behave elastically as linear spring elements under tensile load.

Tribological contact between spherical concave-convex substrates follows Coulomb friction, with maximum static friction torque proportional to normal contact force and contact radius (Mf = mu * N * Rcontact).
Worst-case minimum base stiffness assumes the continuum bends such that only a single drive cable sustains tensile force.

evidence_relevant_to_topic.claim: Continuum robots suffer from low inherent stiffness, especially under high aspect ratio conditions, which limits their payload capacity and manipulation precision.

Twisting multi-strand cables generates axial contraction force and tension significantly greater than conventional linear cable pulling, offering higher normal force for inter-segment friction locking.
Axial shortening of twisted cables conflicts with the fixed structural length of continuum bodies, necessitating an axial retraction compensation mechanism.
A concave-convex-concave spherical interface contact between adjacent substrates converts line contact into spherical surface contact, optimizing normal pressure transmission and friction generation.

An energy-balance-based contraction model accounts for initial inter-strand gap filling and predicts cable retraction significantly more accurately than an equal-volume cylinder model at higher rotation turns.

Under a 2 N radial load, the average stiffness increased by 127% (from 13.47 N/m to 31.5 N/m) and maximum load capacity increased by 231% (from 4.2 N to 13.9 N) using a 4-strand configuration at 15 motor turns.

A three-strand cable configuration exhibits more uniform torsional transmission and concentrated tension distribution than two-strand or four-strand arrangements due to symmetric equilateral triangle packing.

experimental_setup: Resin-fabricated 3-joint bionic spine-like continuum robot prototype (17 substrates total: 6 in joint 1, 6 in joint 2, 5 in joint 3; total length 295 mm, individual substrate lengths 15 mm convex and 20 mm concave, radius 5 mm).
Passive retraction mechanism consisting of a sleeve linked to the drive box and a 4-groove slider with locking bolts to accommodate TSA cable shortening.
Twisted Multi-String Actuator unit utilizing Vectran cables (2-strand, 3-strand, and 4-strand) driven by a dedicated torsion motor and shaft coupling.
Cable retraction test platform measuring contraction length Delta L across varying motor torsion turns N.

Variable stiffness loading test bench configuring the robot as a horizontal cantilever beam, applying radial end loads using calibrated weights (0.5 N increments) while monitoring displacement and cable tension via a dynamometer.
future_work: Develop fully automated, dynamic retraction mechanisms to enable real-time and continuous variable stiffness modulation.
Integrate embedded pose and tension sensors for closed-loop stiffness control.
Explore alternative TSA cable routing and deployment topologies to expand robot workspace and bending curvature range.
Incorporate higher-torque actuation units to further expand load-bearing capacity.
Investigate robot dynamic interaction performance and stability during operational tasks.
independent_variables: Number of TSA cable strands (n = 2, 3, 4)
Number of motor torsion turns (N: up to 30 turns for n=2 and n=3; up to 17 turns for retraction and 15 turns for stiffness tests for n=4)
External radial load applied at the end-effector (F: 0 to ~14 N in 0.5 N increments)
limitations_inferred: Manual loosening and tightening of slider bolts during retraction prevents continuous, in-motion stiffness adaptation during dynamic robotic tasks.
Repeated friction locking between 3D-printed resin spherical interfaces may result in progressive surface wear, changing the friction coefficient over extended cyclic loading.
Static dead-weight loading does not capture dynamic viscoelastic relaxation, vibration damping, or hysteresis of the twisted Vectran cables under high-frequency interaction.
limitations_stated_by_authors: The passive retraction mechanism is not yet fully automated and requires manual loosening and re-tightening of bolts.
Vectran cable rupture occurs under loads greater than 20 N, constraining the safe experimental loading regime to 0-10 N.
Arranging the TSA cable along the central axis restricts the maximum substrate joint bending angle to between 11 and 13 degrees.
Central TSA cable routing provides lower routing flexibility compared to traditional single-cable force-locking schemes.
Stiffness modulation is constrained by the torque limits of the drive motors, causing substrate slippage when external load exceeds maximum friction force.
main_results: The bionic continuum robot achieved omnidirectional bending up to 90 degrees across all directions, validating motion feasibility with joint movement limits of 13 degrees (concave-convex) and 11 degrees (convex-concave).

The theoretical contraction model derived from virtual work/energy balance accurately matched measured multi-strand cable retraction, outperforming the traditional constant-volume model at higher torsion revolutions.

TSA actuation significantly enhanced structural stiffness; for n=4 strands at N=15 turns, average stiffness reached 31.5 N/m compared to 13.47 N/m in the unstiffened baseline (a 127% increase), and maximum failure load rose from 4.2 N to 13.9 N (a 231% increase).
For n=3 strands at N=30 turns, the maximum tolerable load increased by 135% (from 4.0 N to 9.4 N).

Structural failure consistently occurred at an end displacement of approximately 250 mm across all strand configurations, preceded by a slope change at roughly 150 mm indicating partial inter-substrate slip.

Symmetric packing in the 3-strand cable provided optimal torsional transmission uniformity compared to 2-strand (side-overloading tendency) and 4-strand (uneven gap and torque concentration) arrangements.
modeling_methods: Kinematic/geometric modeling of twisted string contraction (cylindrical expansion and helix angle formulation modified for radius expansion).
Energy balance and virtual work modeling of TSA contraction relating motor input torque to cable elastic strain energy.
Cantilever beam structural mechanics modeling with a discrete matrix correction factor (Krobot = 2 * Ebase * Ibase / l^3).
Tribological force-locking formulation deriving inter-substrate spherical contact friction torque from normal forces induced by TSA and drive cables.
Two-state mechanical equilibrium modeling distinguishing between pure static friction (relative rest) and post-slip partial inter-substrate rotation.
Geometric aperture constraint analysis for maximum inter-substrate bending and rotational limit angles.

constitutive_assumptions: Planar (2-D) rigid-link approximation modeling the continuum robot dynamics as an underactuated mechanical system (n > m) under the piecewise constant curvature (PCC) geometric assumption with uniform segment mass and length.
Antagonistic cable tension produces bending where axial deformation is negligible compared to bending deformation.
Air mass inside the airtight membrane is negligible, keeping the gravitational potential parameter α1 constant and independent of vacuum pressure uP.
Elastic potential coefficient α2(uP) depends nonlinearly on vacuum pressure uP, parameterized as a positive quadratic polynomial α2(uP) = c1*uP^2 + c2*uP + c3.
Internal energy dissipation is attributed solely to lumped friction torque with the structural damping matrix set to zero (D(q) = 0).

Pressure along the jamming layer is uniformly distributed with value (-uP), and lumped normal contact force Fn is proportional to a positive, monotonically increasing function φ(uP) = c4 + c5*sqrt(uP).
LuGre friction model parameters satisfy standard physical constraints (static friction coefficient μS >= Coulomb friction coefficient μC > 0) and the passivity condition σ2 > σ1*(μS - μC)/μC.
Motor actuator dynamics in current/torque control mode are negligible compared to continuum robot dynamics, and tensions are uniformly distributed along the cables.
Input matrix satisfies a uniformity condition G(q) = [g(q)*1n, -g(q)*1n] with |g(q)| bounded away from zero.

Actuation: two DYNAMIXEL servo motors (XM430-W350) with customized aluminum spools operating in current regulation mode for direct torque control.

Jamming sheaths: 5-layer sheath tested up to 80 kPa for shape-locking experiments; 2-layer sheath tested up to 40 kPa for stiffness regulation and closed-loop control experiments.

limitations_inferred: The 2-D piecewise constant curvature assumption cannot capture out-of-plane torsional deformations, gravity-induced non-constant curvature under varying spatial orientations, or complex distributed contact along the robot body.
The necessity of switching between 5-layer and 2-layer sheaths indicates an operational trade-off where high locking capacity limits the continuous stiffness-tuning dynamic control range.

Reliance on line-of-sight optical tracking of a single distal AprilTag restricts applicability in cluttered or enclosed operational domains (e.g., minimally invasive surgery or collapsed search-and-rescue voids).
limitations_stated_by_authors: The model and experimental verification are restricted to a single-section prototype in planar (2-D) bending with two tendon inputs (m=2) under rigid-link and piecewise constant curvature (PCC) approximations.

Actuator dynamics and mechanical transmission friction are neglected, causing transient trajectory plateaus when antagonistic net motor torque is temporarily insufficient to overcome stiction and jamming resistance.
Vision-based tracking suffers from transient artifacts (motion blur or image degradation) during motion, creating brief spikes in position estimation.
Using a single distal AprilTag requires assuming uniform curvature (qi = θ) across segments; tracking multiple markers would introduce computational latency and blur.
Empirical parameter fitting for α2(uP) is strictly valid within the tested operating interval ([0, 40] kPa).
Excessive vacuum pressure or higher layer counts can cause unintentional shape locking, hindering dynamic configuration control.
The controller is formulated and validated for setpoint regulation rather than time-varying trajectory tracking.
main_results: Formulated a port-Hamiltonian dynamic model combining rigid-link continuum dynamics with LuGre friction dynamics, theoretically proving the local asymptotic stability of the shape-locking equilibrium manifold and deriving an analytical formula for pressure-dependent overall stiffness K = α1*1n×n + (α2 + σ0*φ(uP))*In.
Experimentally validated shape locking, demonstrating that higher vacuum pressure reduces residual deflection upon tendon release (9.2 mm at 30 kPa, 6.7 mm at 60 kPa, and 3.8 mm at 80 kPa).
Demonstrated that open-loop transverse stiffness follows a square-root dependence on negative pressure φ(uP) = c4 + c5*sqrt(uP) with an empirical coefficient of determination R2 = 0.9216.
Synthesized a passivity-based energy-shaping controller with provable global asymptotic stability for assignable configurations, achieving rapid convergence in under 15 s.
Achieved high configuration regulation accuracy across tested vacuum pressures (0-40 kPa) with steady-state MAE between 0.05 deg and 0.58 deg.

Demonstrated decoupled control of configuration and stiffness: closed-loop stiffness is dominated by vacuum pressure (via σ0*φ(uP)), with the energy-shaping gain γ contributing at most 8.73% and α2 contributing at most 3.55%, and their relative contributions decreasing as pressure increases.

evidence_relevant_to_topic.claim: Layer jamming utilizes overlapping thin plastic or paper sheets enclosed in an airtight membrane where vacuum pressure modulates interlayer friction to produce variable stiffness.

The dynamical behavior of a layer jamming-based, tendon-driven continuum robot can be formulated in port-Hamiltonian form by coupling an energy-based rigid link mechanical model with the LuGre friction model.
The equilibria manifold corresponding to shape locking under constant negative pressure without external actuation is locally asymptotically stable via LaSalle's invariance principle.
The linearized open-loop stiffness matrix at the equilibrium is analytically expressed as a constant structural matrix plus a term directly proportional to the vacuum pressure.
Transverse stiffness measured at the end-effector exhibits a linear correlation with negative pressure, yielding KT = 0.0046*uP + 0.3068 with a determination coefficient of R^2_s = 0.8083.
Shape locking preserves a 60-degree bending configuration upon tendon release, with higher negative pressure reducing steady-state position displacement from 9.2 mm at 30 kPa to 3.8 mm at 80 kPa.

experimental_setup: OctRobot-I continuum robotic platform configured with motor-driven tendon actuation.
Airtight membrane containing a jamming sheath composed of 5 overlapping layers installed over the robot spine.
Transverse stiffness testing apparatus at the end-effector around the open-loop equilibrium under varying negative pressure from 0 to 80 kPa, repeated three times.

Four-phase shape-locking sequence: Phase 1 (initial unactuated state), Phase 2 (tendon driven to 60-degree bending), Phase 3 (vacuum applied at 30 kPa or 80 kPa while holding motor drive), and Phase 4 (vacuum retained while releasing tendon force to zero).
Visual tracking and photographic overlay to measure positional shifts between Phase 3 and Phase 4.
future_work: Synthesizing model-based feedback controllers based on the proposed control-oriented port-Hamiltonian framework.
Revisiting and refining Assumption 3 concerning the relationship between negative pressure and lumped normal force to improve stiffness prediction accuracy.

Tendon tension actuation force u

limitations_inferred: The experimental validation was conducted solely on planar 2D bending up to 60 degrees, leaving 3D spatial bending, torsion, and multi-segment interaction unverified.
Dynamic tracking, cyclic loading, and hysteresis effects during repeated jamming-unjamming transitions were not evaluated.
Assumptions of constant elasticity and negligible membrane mass omit potential non-linear elastomer stretching or material wear under prolonged vacuum cycling.
limitations_stated_by_authors: The overall stiffness matrix K cannot be directly measured experimentally; only transverse stiffness KT at the end-effector could be detected.
The assumed direct proportionality between vacuum pressure and lumped normal force (Assumption 3) requires revision to improve model fitting precision.
The proposed model is oriented toward control design, but closed-loop feedback controller synthesis was not implemented in this study.
main_results: Formulated the first control-oriented port-Hamiltonian dynamical model for layer jamming-based continuum robots combining rigid-link dynamics and the LuGre friction model.
Mathematically proved that shape locking corresponds to a locally asymptotically stable equilibria manifold under constant vacuum pressure.
Analytically established that robot open-loop stiffness scales linearly with applied vacuum pressure: K = alpha1*1_nxn + [alpha2 + sigma0*uP]*In.
Empirically demonstrated a linear relationship between end-effector transverse stiffness and negative pressure (R^2_s = 0.8083, KT = 0.0046*uP + 0.3068 N/mm).
Empirically confirmed that higher vacuum pressure significantly suppresses relaxation displacement during shape locking (3.8 mm at 80 kPa compared to 9.2 mm at 30 kPa).

evidence_relevant_to_topic.claim: Laminar jamming modulates bending stiffness by locking or unlocking thin sheets, transitioning between an uncoupled flexible state where layers slide and a locked rigid state where layers bend as a unified structure.
The theoretical stiffness ratio of laminar jamming structures is proportional to the number of layers squared, though physical friction and lock/unlock mechanism efficacy constrain real-world values.
SMA-wrapped laminar jamming structures achieved a stiffness variation of 60x with a stiffness range of 0.03 to 1.8 N/mm, but are limited by slow heating and cooling times of 100 s and 200 s.

Electrostatic layer jamming mechanisms utilize alternating polarity high-voltage polyimide layers to achieve up to 18x stiffness variation with fast response times under 5 ms actuation and 15 ms release.
Vacuum-pressure-activated laminar jamming is the most prevalent friction-based method, offering stiffness variations between 10x and 180x and a stiffness range from 0.008 to 1.522 N/mm.

Discrete laminar jamming (DLJ) utilizes discrete variable pressure clamps (bolts, rubber bands, or piezoelectric actuators) eliminating the elastic membrane and vacuum sealing issues, demonstrating a 17x stiffness variation.
Mechanical interference mechanisms use actuators (such as SMA or electroactive polymers) to engage teeth into gaps between layers, yielding up to 14.6x stiffness variation.
Laminar jamming structures using heating blankets achieve low stiffness variation (2.25x to 4x) across a high stiffness range of approximately 5 to 18 N/mm, with slow thermal switching speeds.
Sliding-layer laminates (SLL) alternate rigid and soft segments to adjust stiffness by 3x to 7x over a 0.005 to 0.035 N/mm range using linear actuators with ~4 s transition times.

Laminar jamming combined with positive pressure pneumatic actuators (e.g. pneu-nets or McKibben artificial muscles) enables decoupled control of bending shape and structural stiffness in soft robotic grippers and fingers.

Continuum robots employ tubular configurations of overlapping multi-flap Mylar films or mesh sheaths with internal backbone springs to vary bending stiffness for minimally invasive surgery and bioinspired structures.

Wearable robotic applications include soft layer jamming linear brakes (SLJB) and sliding linkage mechanisms providing variable stiffness and braking in axial tension and bending for spinal, elbow, wrist, and finger rehabilitation.

In robot arms, dual parallel-guided beam links containing solid compliant backbones flanked by vacuum laminar jamming jammers improve vertical and torsional stability while providing compliance for impact mitigation.
The trapezoidal pin mechanism combines discrete mechanical clamping with mechanical interference via a pneumatic cylinder to provide variable stiffness while guide frames prevent layer buckling.

Vacuum-activated laminar jamming exhibits a switching time constant of approximately 0.5 s, which is too slow to mitigate active collisions with humans where impact damage occurs in approximately 0.1 s.
Under excessive external loading, vacuum laminar jamming transitions from pre-slip to full-slip regime, dropping stiffness and risking catastrophic yielding if load is maintained.
Finite element analysis (FEA) has demonstrated high fidelity for laminar jamming mechanics with coefficients of determination (R^2) reaching 0.9879 against experimental data.
Recent analytical formulations for arbitrary numbers of layers offer computationally efficient alternatives to FEA where simulation runtime increases substantially with layer count.

evidence_relevant_to_topic.claim: Positive pressure layer jamming significantly increases the bending stiffness of inflated beam robots without requiring a negative pressure / vacuum source.
Three-point bending characterization of a 15-layer paper stack shows an effective flexural modulus of 263.2 kPa in the unjammed state and 3038.6 kPa in the jammed state.
Transverse loading of an inflated beam with jammed versus unjammed segments induces localized buckling at the stiffness boundary, functioning as a discrete revolute joint.

Finite element simulations in ABAQUS using linear elastic material models accurately capture localized buckling when the distal segment is unjammed and cohesive base bending when both segments are jammed.
A triangular wave interface between adjacent jamming pouches prevents premature beam buckling by preventing wrinkle propagation along circumferential circular arcs.
Stiffness patterning enables a single tendon actuator to selectively activate and bend multiple discrete joints sequentially, decoupling controllable degrees of freedom from actuator count.
Paper layer jamming pouches are compatible with tip-everting growth when pouches are unjammed at internal body pressure during growth.

experimental_setup: Instron universal testing machine (Model 3344) for three-point bending of a 15-layer paper stack sealed in TPU-coated ripstop nylon over a 150 mm span at 24 mm/min up to 6 mm displacement.

Transverse bending test rig comprising a cantilever clamp, motorized linear rail translating at 0.2 mm/s, and a Mark-10 Series 5 force gauge with a 3D-printed contact attachment applying up to 10 mm tip deflection.

Joint stiffness test setup equipped with an OptiTrack motion capture camera system (Flex 13 cameras) tracking retroreflective marker patterns on distal and proximal segments of a two-segment inflated beam under transverse loading.
Suspended multi-segment robot demonstration platform with a 1 m long, four-segment inflated beam robot actuated in 3D free space via three motorized Spectra tendons routed through PTFE stoppers.

main_results: The effective material flexural modulus increased by an order of magnitude from 263.2 kPa (unjammed) to 3038.6 kPa (jammed).

Jamming layers produced a substantial increase in transverse beam stiffness: at 6.9 kPa internal pressure, the required transverse force at 10 mm deflection increased by 624% (from 1.07 N to 6.68 N), and at 20.7 kPa internal pressure, it increased by 663%.

Positive pressure jamming at atmospheric pressure achieved stiffness comparable to vacuum jamming (differences of only 4.7% at 13.8 kPa and 2.1% at 20.7 kPa), demonstrating effective stiffness change without an external vacuum source.

Bending tests and FEA confirmed that unjamming a distal segment localizes buckling and rotation to the joint interface while the jammed proximal segment remains straight, whereas jamming both segments causes cohesive bending at the base.

evidence_relevant_to_topic.claim: A tubular stiffening segment utilizing layer jamming can temporarily increase soft robot stiffness under negative pressure, producing an increase in bending stiffness of over 15x at 0 degrees, over 30x at 90 degrees, and up to 60x in compressive stiffness at -60 kPa.

A bio-inspired flexible spine featuring rigid ABS vertebrae integrated with an elastomeric soft continuum robot prevents cross-sectional buckling and maintains segment diameter during bending (achieving a diameter ratio of 0.981 at 180 degrees compared to 0.856 for an unreinforced soft continuum robot).

An analytical mechanics model dividing layer jamming shear behavior into pre-slip, transition, and full-slip regimes captures the effective stiffness variation with applied vacuum pressure, achieving a minimum determination coefficient (R^2) of 0.9525 relative to experimental data.

The tuneable-stiffness soft continuum robot demonstrates an adjustable length range of 185.35 mm to 363.35 mm, a bending angle reaching 196 degrees, and peak load support of 31.45 N under operational pressures of +/-60 kPa.
